slides: Let's continue with quadrilaterals, and meet the whole family.

slides.say: So which kinds of quadrilaterals are there? What do you remember from school? There's the ordinary quadrilateral, and then a whole family of special ones. Let's see how one turns into another.

Here's a square, a perfect quadrilateral, with all its sides equal. Take a square and stretch it a little, and you get a rectangle. The angles are still right angles, but now only the opposite sides are equal.
Now take a rectangle and step on it, squash it a bit to the side, and you get a parallelogram. The opposite sides stay parallel and equal, but the angles aren't right angles any more.

Now take a parallelogram and shorten its two longer sides, until all four sides are equal. The opposite sides stay parallel. It becomes a rhombus. I know it doesn't really look like one, because it's lying down. We're used to seeing a rhombus like on playing cards, standing on a corner. So let's turn it a little. Now it really looks like a rhombus.
You can also squash a square a bit, and get a rhombus. All four sides stay equal.

Take a rhombus and pull its bottom corner down, and you get a kite, also called a deltoid. A kite has two equal sides next to each other. The other two sides are equal too. In this picture, the top pair is shorter. All four sides can also be equal, as in a rhombus.
And take a rectangle, and move its two top corners toward each other, and you get a trapezoid. Its top and bottom stay parallel, but the other two sides are no longer parallel.
So those are all our quadrilaterals, and how one turns into another. The name of a shape carries a lot of information, so when a question names the shape, underline it.
at: when a question names the shape

slides.say: Now the same family as a tree. Read every line going down as a special kind of. At the top is the general quadrilateral. A trapezoid, a parallelogram and a kite are special kinds of quadrilateral.
at: A trapezoid, a parallelogram and a kite

slides.say: A rectangle is a special parallelogram, a parallelogram with right angles. A rhombus is a special parallelogram, and also a special kite, with all four sides equal. And at the bottom is the square. It's a rectangle and a rhombus at the same time.
at: A rectangle is a special parallelogram

slides.say: Going down a line of the tree, a shape only gains properties. So a square has all the rectangle rules. It also has all the rhombus rules. But knowing that a shape is a rectangle doesn't guarantee that it's a square.
For example, every square is a rectangle, because it has four right angles. But a rectangle is not necessarily a square. This rectangle is three by two, so its sides are not all equal.
at: This rectangle is three by two

slides.say: That's why we say not necessarily. A rhombus is always a parallelogram, but a kite is not necessarily a rhombus. From here, there's a lesson on each shape. We start with the square, the easiest to understand, because we all know what a square is. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next video.
at: That's why we say not necessarily
